overview.title: Welcome to Go for reMarkable 👋

sections.text: All the pages, in reading order

overview.text: Welcome to Go for reMarkable 👋 Go for reMarkable runs Go programs on the reMarkable Paper Pro : an interface on paper that stays still until you touch it, ink that follows the pen, and a screen that turns with the tablet. It is the tablet's side of the family: the program's loop, the pen and the fingers, and the tools that put a program on the tablet. Go UI builds the interface and Go Renderer turns it into shapes. An e-ink panel has no graphics chip to speak of, so here the shapes are blended by the processor, and only the pixels that changed reach the panel. 🚧 An experiment. What was checked says exactly what ran on a real tablet. Is it for me? ✅ You have a reMarkable Paper Pro in developer mode and want to put your own program on it. ✅ You want to see how to write for e-ink , where every change of the picture has a price. ❌ You have a reMarkable 2 or a Paper Pro Move: their screens are different, and nothing here was made for them. ❌ You want something that survives updates by itself: this depends on xovi and AppLoad, which follow each version of the tablet's software. Where to start Pick the line that sounds like you. If you… Read Time are new and want a program on the tablet 📜 The quest : from words on paper to your own program, in 5 levels 45 min want to know what each package does and what you need What is where 10 min plan a larger program Before writing a larger program 5 min All the pages, in reading order The menu on the left (or the files in docs/ ) follows this order. Start Overview : this page The quest : five levels, from words on paper to turning the tablet What is where : the packages, the tools, what you need, what was checked, and what is not done yet 🚧 Not done yet See what is where . Words you will meet Word What it means Go A programming language. To try these projects you install it once, from go.dev. Terminal The window where you type commands: Terminal on macOS and Linux, PowerShell on Windows. Developer mode A setting of the tablet that lets you open a terminal on it over USB, with SSH. xovi A tool that adds extensions to the tablet's own program. It stays off until you start it, and a restart turns it off again. AppLoad The xovi extension that lists and opens programs like these. E-ink A screen of tiny capsules that keeps its picture with no power, and pays for every change. Refresh The moment the panel changes its capsules. Fast ones leave a ghost of the old picture; clean ones take longer. Quest The tutorial of these docs: short levels, each ending with something that works and an achievement. The family Go for reMarkable is one of a family of small projects that work together: Project What it does Go Renderer draws 3D scenes and flat interfaces Go UI buttons, panels and whole applications Go UI for Android Android apps that look like Android's own Go Sound sound and music Go Scene Builder 3D scenes from a flat map Go Simulator simulations that change a scene Go Terrain Simulator ground shaped by rivers Go Climate Simulator weather and biomes Go Flora Simulator forests that grow Go Urban Simulator towns that grow Go Motion Simulator a scene that moves Go for 3DS Go on the Nintendo 3DS Go for Meta Quest Go on the Meta Quest 3 Go for reMarkable (this one) Go on the reMarkable Paper Pro ⚠️ All of them are educational experiments , written with an AI assistant and pending review by their author: good for learning and playing, not for production.

the-quest.title: The paper quest
the-quest.text: The paper quest Put a Go program on a reMarkable Paper Pro, one level at a time. Each level teaches one piece of Go for reMarkable and ends with a program you open on the tablet. We start by making the tablet ready, then put words on paper, count presses of a button without wasting a refresh, write with the pen, and finally turn the tablet and watch the interface follow. Every level has the same shape: the idea , the code , and a checkpoint to know it works. Before you start You need: Why Where Go 1.26 or later The compiler; it builds for the tablet by itself go.dev A reMarkable Paper Pro in developer mode, and a USB-C cable Where it runs The tablet's settings xovi and AppLoad They list and open programs xovi , AppLoad Clone the repository; Go fetches Go UI and Go Renderer by itself. git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-remarkable cd go-remarkable ⚠️ This is your tablet, at your own risk. Follow xovi's and AppLoad's own instructions, for exactly your version of the tablet's software. Nothing here writes to the system partition, so leaving is a restart away: xovi stops, and the tablet is as it was. Each time you restart the tablet, xovi is off. Over SSH ( ssh root@10.11.99.1 ), start it like this: systemctl mask --runtime rm-emergency.service systemctl show rm-emergency.service -p LoadState # must say LoadState=masked; if not, stop here systemctl reset-failed xochitl /home/root/xovi/start The first line matters. If the tablet's own program fails while xovi is starting, the system's reaction is an emergency restart. --runtime turns that reaction off only until the next restart. ✅ Checkpoint: after half a minute the tablet shows its usual screen, and AppLoad is in the side menu. Level 1 · Words on paper The idea. AppLoad is a shelf. It looks in a folder for programs, and each one comes with a small label, external.manifest.json , that gives its name. When you open one, AppLoad hands it a piece of screen, and the program paints it. The code. A program only has to say how to draw itself. This is the heart of cmd/hello/main.go : func newProgram(app.Device) app.Program { return app.Program{Draw: draw} } func draw(context *ui.Context) { context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(marginInLayoutPixels)}, func() { context.Heading("Hello, paper") }) } main only calls app.Run(newProgram) . Build it and send it over: tools/build.sh ./cmd/hello # prints out/hello tools/install.sh out/hello # prints installed hello on root@10.11.99.1 Reload AppLoad's list and open Hello, paper . ✅ Checkpoint: the words are on the panel, and they stay there with the program asleep. 🏅 Achievement: first ink, without a pen. Level 2 · A button that counts The idea. A phone repaints sixty times a second and nobody minds. E-ink pays for every change, with time and with ghosts of the old picture. So the program sleeps until something happens, and it sends only the pixels that changed. Go UI's usual button also darkens while it is held. On paper that is a whole extra refresh before anything has happened, so paper.Button keeps one look. The code , from cmd/counter/main.go : func (shown *counter) draw(context *ui.Context) { context.Box(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(marginInLayoutPixels), Gap: gapInLayoutPixels}, func() { context.Heading(fmt.Sprintf("Pressed %d times", shown.count)) if paper.Button(context, addButtonName) { shown.count++ } }) } tools/build.sh ./cmd/counter && tools/install.sh out/counter ✅ Checkpoint: each press changes the number, once. Nothing flashes while your finger is down. You can prove it with no tablet at all. apptest replaces AppLoad with a stand-in that remembers what it was asked, and cmd/counter/main_test.go checks that a press costs exactly one refresh: go test ./cmd/counter 🏅 Achievement: thrifty painter. Level 3 · Writing The idea. Building a whole interface for each point of a pen would be far too slow for handwriting. So ink.Surface takes the pen away from the interface and paints straight on the canvas, in the fastest refresh mode. When the pen rests for two seconds, the lines get one clean refresh. Your palm can rest on the panel meanwhile: while the pen writes, touches are ignored. AppLoad does not tell a program how hard you press, so pen reads the pen's own device, without taking it away from the system. The code , from cmd/notebook/main.go . The program makes the paper, shows it, and tells the loop that it has one: func (shown *notebook) draw(context *ui.Context) { context.Box(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(marginInLayoutPixels), Gap: gapInLayoutPixels}, func() { if paper.Button(context, clearButtonName) { shown.page.Clear() } shown.page.DrawPaper(context) }) } func newProgram(device app.Device) app.Program { shown := &notebook{page: device.NewInk()} return app.Program{Draw: shown.draw, Ink: shown.page} } tools/build.sh ./cmd/notebook && tools/install.sh out/notebook ✅ Checkpoint: the line follows the tip. Press harder and it gets wider. Turn the pen over, and a band shows what the eraser is about to remove; lift it and that part is gone. 🏅 Achievement: pen pal. Level 4 · Turn the tablet The idea. The tablet already knows which way up it is. AppLoad passes that on, if the program says in its label that it can turn: { "name": "Notebook", "application": "notebook", "qtfb": true, "supportsRotation": true } There is nothing to add to the code: app turns the canvas, the pen and the fingers, and the strokes stay where they are on the panel. One catch is easy to miss. AppLoad opens a program in a window , and a window turns only with its own button. Only in full screen does it follow the tablet. ✅ Checkpoint: open the notebook, press AppLoad's full-screen button, and turn the tablet each way. The button moves to the new top, and taps still land on it. 🏅 Achievement: right way up, whichever that is. Level 5 · Everything at once The idea. cmd/demo is a test bench with one screen for each thing the tablet can do: reading, buttons, ink, gestures, the panel's refresh modes, and a monitor of every event. It is also the example to read for the rest of app.Program : RefreshMode picks how each frame reaches the panel, InkOpen says when the paper is on screen, and OnEvent sees everything first. tools/build.sh ./cmd/demo && tools/install.sh out/demo ✅ Checkpoint: on Screen , press each mode and compare what the patch leaves behind. 🏅 Achievement: knows the panel by heart. 🏁 Your own program Copy cmd/counter to cmd/<your-program> , change application in the manifest to that same folder name, and draw something of your own. For what an interface for paper can look like, read cmd/library : a shelf, a page that stays still until it is turned, and a notebook, with real prints for covers and nothing that moves. Before you do anything long, read before writing a larger program .

what-is-where.title: What is where

sections.text: How a frame gets to the panel

what-is-where.text: What is where The packages of Go for reMarkable, the programs and tools it comes with, what you need, and what was checked on a real tablet. What is where Piece What it does app The program loop: app.Run opens the screen and answers events until AppLoad closes the program. A program is an app.Program , and only Draw is required. Between events it sleeps. qtfb The connection to AppLoad: pixels in shared memory, a socket for refreshes, input events, the refresh modes and the tablet's rotation. canvas The frame, composed on the processor. It blends Go Renderer's shapes, turns for each orientation, and copies to the panel only the pixels that changed. ink ink.Surface , paper to write on: lines that follow the pen with no interface in between, an eraser, and a clean refresh when the pen rests. pen The pen's pressure, tilt and eraser, read from its own device, which is never taken from the system. If it cannot be read, ink still works with plain lines. pointer Turns the tablet's pen and fingers into the single pointer an interface expects, and copes with a resting palm and with presses whose release never came. paper A calm look for e-ink: a theme of soft ink and thin lines on pure white, and buttons, a switch, cards and a progress bar that cost no extra refresh when touched. keys Turns the keys of a physical keyboard, such as the Type Folio, into text and editing keys. AppLoad sends the same code for "a" and "A", so it keeps track of Shift, Caps Lock and accents itself. apptest Runs a program with no tablet: a stand-in for AppLoad that remembers what it was asked, and events delivered by hand. failure Errors with a stable name, such as qtfb.server-not-found , to check with errors.Is . cmd/hello , cmd/counter , cmd/notebook The small programs of the quest . cmd/library The example of a finished interface: a shelf of books, a reader and a notebook. cmd/demo The test bench: Reading, Buttons, Ink, Gestures, Screen and Monitor. Each screen logs what it cost. tools/build.sh Builds ./cmd/<program> for the tablet into out/<program> , with its manifest. tools/install.sh Copies out/<program> into AppLoad's folder over SSH. It writes only inside the program's own folder. REMARKABLE_HOST changes where it goes. How a frame gets to the panel your Draw → Go UI → Go Renderer's painter → canvas → only what changed → AppLoad → panel Ink takes a short cut, because a pen cannot wait for an interface: the pen → ink.Surface → canvas → that small area → AppLoad → panel The first picture is built twice per update, because a press changes what the next build shows, and it reaches the panel only if the frame looks different from the last one. What you need Go 1.26 or later. The programs are pure Go, so tools/build.sh needs nothing else. A reMarkable Paper Pro in developer mode, reachable over SSH. xovi and AppLoad on it, started as in the quest . xovi's table of names must be built for your exact version of the tablet's software. go.mod pins Go UI and Go Renderer at commits of theirs, until they release what this uses. What was checked On a Paper Pro with software 3.29.1.0 and a build of AppLoad's main branch, the demo was tried by hand, before it was divided into these packages: What Result Reading and Buttons Good. A tap costs one frame of about 150 ms up to sending the refresh. Ink Follows the pen and comes out clean; pressure, tilt and eraser were felt to work; a palm breaks nothing. Gestures, Monitor All respond. Screen The turn button keeps taps in the right place; Fast sometimes looks greyer. Turning the tablet All four positions, in full screen. AppLoad's own gestures The swipe from the top and five fingers leave the program working. At rest All six screens stayed at 0 % processor with no frames, for 30 seconds each. Not run on a tablet: cmd/hello , cmd/counter , cmd/notebook , cmd/library , tools/build.sh and tools/install.sh as they stand here, nor the demo since it became packages. The tests run the same code with a stand-in for AppLoad. The demo's two-finger list and its swipe to the end, and the eraser's band at its final width, were installed but not reported on. Before writing a larger program Changing the refresh mode costs a second. AppLoad reads nothing more from a program for a second after each change. Keep one mode per screen. The mode you set is read later, when the panel repaints, so do not set it back straight after a refresh. Modes above qtfb.Interface close the connection. AppLoad takes five, and hangs up on the rest. The refresh is not the end. The times logged stop at sending it; AppLoad never says when the panel has finished. Some gestures are AppLoad's. A swipe from the top edge opens its bar, and five fingers force a full refresh. Input can be messy. AppLoad v0.6.0 reports a finger that did not move as another press; its main branch fixes that. A system menu can keep a finger's release for itself. pointer copes with both. Follow the tablet's conventions. On the rest of the tablet two fingers scroll, and a swipe down goes to the end of the page. cmd/demo/gestures.go shows how. In a window, nothing turns by itself. See level 4 . Not yet Only the Paper Pro. The panel's size and pixel format are written into app and qtfb . canvas paints no frosted backdrops, so Go UI's glass does not show. A program cannot save what is written yet: strokes live in memory. Text comes only from a physical keyboard. Nothing brings up the on-screen one, and keys has not been tried on the tablet yet. No desktop runner in this repository: besides the tablet, there is only apptest . Once, before these packages, the tablet's input stopped reaching a program for minutes. It did not come back in later tries, and its cause is unknown.
